content:
#1 I’ve been interacting quite a bit of late with LLMs and it’s raising some questions for me about the wiki. Of course you have to be very cautious about LLM outputs, but they seem really quite useful already when trying to think through how to use a concept. One would imagine that in another few years they’ll be the go-to for most people trying to learn about new mathematical concepts.

Now, answers at the moment frequently refer to nLab pages, so it’s clear that the nLab has played a powerful role in shaping the training of LLMs. One might think that looking forward, providing a site of secure information is a primary goal, both for those interacting directly with its pages and for the future training of accurate LLMs. Business as usual in either case.

On the other hand, if LLMs are tending to greater accuracy, greater self-correction, etc., it’s not then completely obvious what the writing strategy should be. I could imagine a voice from the AI-optimism side which would see a limited role for humans condensing collective wisdom concerning mathematical concepts on wiki pages, when there are already AI devices trained on all of that collective wisdom and ready to answer queries interactively at whatever level of sophistication required.

Any thoughts? For one thing I’d like to know whether/how people here are using LLMs in their research.
subject: nLab in the era of LLMs

content:
#4 I see in this latest breakthrough in combinatorics, The sum-product conjecture is false for real numbers, that the authors write:

The role of AI in this proof. The authors were inspired to revisit the possibility of disproving the sum-product conjecture using number fields of large degree by the recent OpenAI counterexample to the unit distance conjecture (see [2]). Curiously, the final construction given here required far less number theoretic input than the unit distance counterexample. GPT-5.5 Pro was used as a sounding board in the early stages of the development of this proof, but the final proof, including all the main ideas, was almost entirely human-generated (the exception being the suggestion of Lemma 3.4, which replaced a more complicated result of Schinzel with a short elementary argument). Everything in this paper was written by the authors.

I wouldn’t mind betting that this “sounding board” use will become very prevalent as time goes on, perhaps unacknowledged. It’s the capacity to act in this way in the kinds of fields we cover here that arises from training on our pages.

content:
#28 Hard to find the central thread in this discussion, but I gather it’s about the future of mathematics, and of the nLab, in the dawning age of AI.

 \,

On the future of mathematics:

The steam engine revolutionized transport. Back then, if you were strictly into the horse part of horse carriages, you went out of business. But if your concern was transportation beyond horses, you received an enormous boost.

Feynman was famously fond of showing off his mental arithmetic skill. Impressive as that was, nobody feels it as a loss that the pocket calculator made it obsolete — it simply freed us to focus on far more interesting tasks.

In this vein, mathematics as such is about to be boosted — empowered to progress further and faster. Just the “horse-riding” routines of math activity will follow mental arithmetic into becoming recreational activity.

It is telling that the conjectures being solved by AI tools these days are ones I have never even heard of before. The deep structural problems remain wide open.

But now we have a formidable new power tool to mount the attack, making progress that was previously unthinkable finally reachable.

Emphasis on tool: A broad misconception appears to be that AI just takes over, like expecting a power drill to build your garage by itself.

 \,

On the future of the nLab:

With or without AI, the nLab’s main bottleneck remains a shortage of substantial human contributions.

But AI can help to scrutinize entries in all kinds of aspects, that’s useful.

content:
#29 People typically think of the nLab as a mathematics wiki, but it is also a physics and philosophy wiki as well. And so I think some things have to be said about LLMs with regards to physics as well.

Recently, Google DeepMind published a paper titled “LLMs can’t jump” which says that while LLMs right now are good at inductive reasoning and deductive reasoning, there is a third part of science that they cannot do, abductive reasoning. So while LLMs can prove things given axioms and infer things given probable assumptions, it cannot create good scientific hypotheses to explain data, so the creation of scientific hypotheses is likely to remain the purview of human scientists.

In particular, in so far as the nLab is a research space for Urs Schreiber and a few others to develop new ideas for phenomena in topological quantum computing and related fields, that purpose will not likely be replaced by LLMs any time soon.

This is probably also applicable in mathematics as well. I think there is a lot of abductive reasoning used to create axioms for branches of synthetic mathematics (like synthetic differential geometry and synthetic algebraic geometry) and the foundations of mathematics, and if LLMs are hopeless with abductive reasoning, then perhaps there will remain a role for mathematicians moving forwards in the actively creative parts of the mathematics.

#35

I know some people weren’t happy with Tim Gowers’ Two Cultures of Mathematics idea, problem-solving and theory-building, but the distinction lines up neatly with the fields of what is being solved, combinatorics over, say, algebraic geometry.

The nCafe isn’t as active as it once was two decades ago, but perhaps it might be worth revisiting the topic of Gowers’s two cultures of mathematics in a blog post over in that community in light of the recent advances in large language models.

Problems there require combining a bunch of techniques in novel ways. There’s no great panorama to unfold. Problems are often disconnected from each other, although patterns of technique combination for one problem can be developed into new combinations for others.

More generally, one thing large language models might have an advantage over humans is perhaps using techniques from one subfield to another subfield. Most mathematicians are experts at only one particular subfield in mathematics and the techniques in that particular subfield. Because of that specialisation, it is really difficult for mathematicians to take techniques from a different subfield, because they then have to spend years to learn in depth about that other subfield, and they are not necessarily guaranteed to get any useful techniques from the years of studying. And there are so many subfields to mine techniques from and apply them to a different subfield, unexplored by humans. Large language models are generalists in mathematics; they basically know about every single subfield in mathematics and the techniques used in the subfields, and so it is much easier for them to use techniques from one subfield and apply them to another subfield.

content:
#36

I know some people weren’t happy with Tim Gowers’ Two Cultures of Mathematics idea, problem-solving and theory-building, but the distinction lines up neatly with the fields of what is being solved, combinatorics over, say, algebraic geometry.

Large language models just proved that non-sofic groups exist by constructing a non-sofic group. I don’t think that the distinction on problems that are hard vs easy for LLMs really aligns with the fields considered to be part of the two cultures of mathematics, if LLMs are constructing new types of objects in group theory and constructing counterexamples in algebraic geometry. Maybe you still have the alignment of LLM ability to prove conjectures with the two cultures of mathematics, but recognize that these two cultures create a divide in every field in mathematics, not just between fields in mathematics.

I’ve said on Kevin Buzzard’s blog that I think the real distinction is between trying to prove existential statements vs trying to prove statements for all elements of a specific type; i.e. the distinction between existential quantification and universal quantification. LLMs are really good at the first kind of conjecture regardless of field, and still pretty terrible at the second kind of conjecture regardless of field.

LLMs also seem to be better at constructive proofs than mere existence proofs, since most of the proofs or refutations are done by constructing a specific object. This probably has implications for constructivism in the philosophy of mathematics. More broadly, LLMs plus the proof assistants are probably going to keep philosophers of mathematicians well employed for the next five decades.

content:
#41 Going back to the original post,

Any thoughts? For one thing I’d like to know whether/how people here are using LLMs in their research.

You have to be really careful when using LLMs for anything mathematics research, because otherwise the LLMs will just assume you are using ZFC as your metatheory by default, and well if your metatheory isn’t ZFC then the LLMs will be asserting things to be true when they are not provable or false in your metatheory, and false when they are not provable or true in your metatheory.

I got bitten by that yesterday when asking about Reinhardt cardinals in well-pointed toposes and the LLMs keep on saying that the topos cannot be well-pointed, which really confused me, since ZF with a Reinhardt cardinal yields a well-pointed topos. When I, much later in the day, asked for a proof, they used the axiom of choice in the metatheory to show any well-pointed topos has to satisfy choice. Well, except the whole point for me when studying Reinhardt cardinals is that you use a metatheory without choice so that models of set theory stay consistent and your category of sets stays well-pointed. So it was a complete waste of a few hours of my life, because LLMs don’t seem to understand the norms of mathematicians studying such large cardinals and just assumed ZFC as a metatheory.

Edit: In the context of constructive mathematics, LLMs will also tend to assume axioms like countable choice and say stuff like LPO is inconsistent with all functions on the Dedekind real numbers being continuous. You have to explicitly say to assume absolutely no choice if you don’t want it to assume countable choice.

In the end, I’ve found large language models to be unreliable. It will confidently say something is true in one moment, then a while later it will start confidently saying that the opposite is true. For example, I asked what the relation between the Cauchy real numbers and the real numbers defined in the HoTT book were, and initially the LLMs said that that the Cauchy real numbers were a subset of the real numbers defined in the HoTT book, and after a few more questions, it started insisting that the the real numbers defined in the HoTT book were a subset of the Cauchy real numbers. Something similar happened with the large cardinals previously as well. Also, even if you insist to assume that the Cauchy real numbers and Dedekind real numbers do not coincide, it will still say stuff like LPO is inconsistent with all functions on the Dedekind real numbers being continuous, despite the fact that there exist toposes where LPO hold and where all functions on the Dedekind real numbers are continuous. It’s like the LLMs are either clueless stochastic parrots who don’t actually understand the subject, or messing with me on purpose, but either way, they’re unreliable.

#47 Colleague in the sense of you’re a research mathematician at a university or similar and you’re talking with other mathematicians who are also doing research at that level.

For a lot of the weaker large language models though, it’s a lot less like a colleague and a lot more like an overconfident undergraduate who read up on a lot of subjects on a surface level but doesn’t truly understand the material. You have to be the expert and be assertive and correct them when they make mistakes, since they do make mistakes frequently. Now this works well enough when you’re talking about subjects that you understand well that you know what’s right and what’s wrong, but it is terrible when you yourself are trying to learn about subjects first hand. Those weaker LLMs are pretty bad teachers because they make many mistakes and contradict their own past statements and you can’t put your trust in them. This is especially the case if you are just restricted to using the free tier (which will likely be the case for most mathematicians); I highly doubt the free tier will be running the latest frontier version of ChatGPT or Claude Fable or whatever.

On the available models:

  • Gemini Pro is available for 22$/month. This is good for literature search (due to its huge context window; in addition Gemini Notebook allows to dig through huge chunks of uploaded literature) and for image generation (such as for slides as I did here).

  • Claude Pro is available for 15–18$/month. This gives you access to Opus 5 for deep math reasoning.

Either — or both combined, that still makes just ∼\sim∼40$/month — gives you all the research assistant power you can dream of. (What a time to be alive.)

The more costly higher tier plans mainly just add additional token volume/priority.

But if on some day you really do run out of tokens, and you are desperate for more tokens, you can still buy a parallel 20$ plan just for that month.

Myself, I have one private Gemini Pro account and one via my institute, and sometimes if I exhaust one I just continue on the other, instead of switching to the 10×\times× as expensive “Ultra” plan.

In short, for the price of a daily sandwich, you get all the available research assistance you could dream of.

content:
#56

Madeleine, I apologize for being a nitpicker but your comment about chess engines is not correct. By 2016 chess engines had thoroughly outclassed humans and didn’t make any human-exploitable mistakes. Komodo had a rating of 3330+ elo compared to Carlsen’s peak of 2882. In 2005 or 2004 it would be truer, but that was more with grandmasters rather than ordinary experts.

No, I’m not talking about overall strength of the chess engines, but weaknesses in the chess engines in specific specialized subfields of chess theory, such as opening theory and heavily positional maneuvering games. in 2016, chess engines were still using handcrafted evaluation functions and so frequently made mistakes in those areas, that the top grandmasters were able to point out. Yes, even with the poor positional play, the tactical strength and search depth of chess engines in 2016 was strong enough to overpower human grandmasters.

For an extreme example of good positional play not correlating with being able to defeat grandmasters, today there is a version of Stockfish called SimpleEval which is rated around 3200 elo (so stronger than all human grandmasters) and its evaluation function is just simple material counting (Pawn = 1, Knight = Bishop = 3, Rook = 5, Queen = 9). If you watch SimpleEval play, it will make a lot of positional mistakes that even amateur club chess players can point out, but that doesn’t really matter for winning games when the engine can reach immense search depths and out calculate the human.

Those issues in positional play for chess engines only went away starting in 2017/18 with AlphaZero and Leela using deep neural network based evaluation functions, and later for Stockfish in 2020 with NNUE. Fabiano Caruana in particular went on a huge run of success in chess tournaments in 2019 because he was one of the first grandmasters to adopt Leela for preparing openings while everybody else was still using Stockfish with a handcrafted evaluation function.

content:
#57 I said above

In the context of constructive mathematics, LLMs will also tend to assume axioms like countable choice and say stuff like LPO is inconsistent with all functions on the Dedekind real numbers being continuous. You have to explicitly say to assume absolutely no choice if you don’t want it to assume countable choice.

and

Also, even if you insist to assume that the Cauchy real numbers and Dedekind real numbers do not coincide, it will still say stuff like LPO is inconsistent with all functions on the Dedekind real numbers being continuous, despite the fact that there exist toposes where LPO hold and where all functions on the Dedekind real numbers are continuous. It’s like the LLMs are either clueless stochastic parrots who don’t actually understand the subject, or messing with me on purpose, but either way, they’re unreliable.

This isn’t actually true in all cases. If you begin with talking about the initial σ\sigmaσ-frame, then the LLMs for some reason assume you’re working in neutral constructive mathematics. And if you begin by asking the LLMs about the difference between the usual Dedekind reals vs the Dedekind reals constructed using Dedekind cuts valued in the initial σ\sigmaσ-frame and how they don’t coincide under LPO, then the LLMs will say that LPO is consistent with all functions on the usual Dedekind real numbers being continuous; they will also say that the usual Dedekind real numbers and the Cauchy real numbers do not coincide with each other either. So LLMs’ responses seem to be very much prompt dependent, and thus, still unreliable unless you are an expert at the subject and are able to guide the LLMs with good prompts and correct the LLMs’ mistakes.

(Note that this is with the free versions of LLMs.)

content:
#60 I wrote above earlier:

I’ve said on Kevin Buzzard’s blog that I think the real distinction is between trying to prove existential statements vs trying to prove statements for all elements of a specific type; i.e. the distinction between existential quantification and universal quantification. LLMs are really good at the first kind of conjecture regardless of field, and still pretty terrible at the second kind of conjecture regardless of field.

If this was true back in May and June of this year, it is no longer true in October. OpenAI’s large language models are apparently able to prove things like no zeros of the Riemann zeta function with real part 78\frac{7}{8}87​ and the Hodge conjecture for all CM abelian varieties, which are both statements involving the universal quantifier, proving for all elements of a specific type.
